problems.stem: You want the page title that shows in the browser tab to read 'Maria Lopez | Portfolio'. Which markup is correct?
problems.explanation: The browser tab text comes from the <title> element inside <head>. <h1> shows on the page itself; it does not set the tab.

problems.stem: Your CSS file has two rules in this order: 'p { color: blue; }' then 'p { color: green; }'. A paragraph with no other styles renders what color?
options: Blue, because it was defined first
Green, because for equal specificity the later rule wins
Black, because the two rules cancel out
Red, the browser default for conflicts
problems.explanation: When two selectors have the same specificity, the rule that appears later in the stylesheet overrides the earlier one, so the text is green.

problems.stem: A coding assistant (such as GitHub Copilot in VS Code, or ChatGPT/Claude) gives you CSS that styles your nav bar but targets a class .container that does not exist in your HTML. What should you do before pasting it in?
options: Paste it as-is; the AI already tested it
Check which selectors match elements that actually exist in my HTML, then add or remove the .container class so the markup and CSS agree
Delete all my existing CSS so there are no conflicts
Keep the unused .container rule because more CSS is safer
problems.explanation: AI-generated CSS often references classes that are not in your HTML. You stay responsible for making selectors and markup match before the styles will do anything.

problems.stem: You write for your About page. A reviewer using a screen reader cannot tell what the image is. What is the correct fix?
options: Make the image larger with width="600"
Add a descriptive alt attribute:
Wrap the image in a <b> tag
problems.explanation: A screen reader announces the alt text. Adding alt="Maria Lopez, headshot" makes the image meaningful to non-visual users; size and format do not address accessibility.
